**Eval validity is the theme today.** Several papers ask whether the numbers we trust measure what we think they do.

The sharpest is the reproducibility audit of LLM/agent vulnerability-validation artifacts (2608.09567). Of 104 papers, only 59 had reachable artifacts. Only 10 of 18 workflows ran end-to-end, and 58 of 102 anchor cases had CVE IDs that disagreed with their directory labels. The embedded oracles were weak: 20 of 30 patched counterfactuals still fired, which gives about 60% sensitivity and 45% specificity. A vulnerable-build trigger isn't CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched control. The same message comes from the threat-preserving representation sensitivity paper (2610.03585). Swapping threat-related for neutral names, with task, harmful action and policy held fixed, moves ASR meaningfully on ASB, MCPTox and AgentDojo. A single ASR number is partly a property of the benchmark's surface form. The DeepSeek Harness indirect-injection study (2608.16393) points the same way. Across 14,560 runs the worst channels reached 16–25% ASR, and the LLM judge counted far more partial compliance than the rule judge (7.3% vs 2.0%). COPEX (2610.04378) is useful for the same reason: it fixes the agent stack and varies only the model across MCP layers, and it reports 64.4% mean ASR over nine models. Taken together, I'd discount any agent-security ASR that comes without a representation or judge sensitivity check.

stories.title: From Runnable to Verifiable: An Independent Reproducibility Study of LLM/Agent-Driven Vulnerability Validation Artifacts
stories.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
stories.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.
stories.reason: ActBench proposes an execution-trajectory-based behavioral safety benchmark for cowork agents, directly applicable to evaluating agent risks like data leakage and unauthorized actions—highly relevant for tooling and red-teaming.

stories.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
stories.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
stories.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
stories.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

stories.title: Security Assessment of DeepSeek Harness with A.I.G: Evaluating Resistance to Indirect Prompt Injection
stories.summary: This work evaluates indirect prompt injection against DeepSeek Harness using AI-Infra-Guard to generate tests, deliver controlled taint across 16 channels and two carrier modes, run 14,560 executions, and analyze traces with both rule-based and LLM-based judges. The strongest observed attack success rates are 17.0% under LLMJudge for a fake-completion attack (text), 25.5% under RuleJudge for hidden Unicode (file), and 16.0% under RuleJudge for the skills channel (file), with LLMJudge assigning more partial compliance than RuleJudge (7.3% vs. 2.0%). The study connects outcomes to DSH’s handling of tool results, extra contexts, and tool-call policy hooks, and proposes controls between untrusted content and sensitive actions, with code released at the linked repository.
stories.why_it_matters: Provides a large-scale, reproducible, channel- and payload-stratified benchmark of indirect prompt injection on an agentic LLM stack with dual judges, informing defense design and evaluation baselines.
stories.reason: Black-box auditing of vendor-hosted LLM APIs via statistical repeated-query testing is highly relevant for red-teaming, API threat models, and evaluation methodology.

stories.title: LiveHouse-TS: An Open-world Living Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models
stories.summary: The paper introduces LiveHouse-TS, an open-world, living benchmark infrastructure for evaluating TSFMs via prequential testing on real future data rather than static windows. It shifts evaluation focus from snapshot accuracy to continuous temporal validity in environments with seasonality, distribution shifts, and unexpected events, aiming to answer long-term questions about ranking stability and robustness. Streaming evaluations across 11 domains and 17 datasets show that model rankings from static benchmarks dramatically reshuffle under the live protocol.
stories.why_it_matters: If you work on LLM security or TSFMs, this exposes how static benchmarks can mislead robustness assessments under shifts, offering an infrastructure to stress-test models’ long-term validity—analogous to live red-teaming and continual evals in LLMs.
stories.reason: Directly targets time-series foundation models with a new open-world benchmark capturing distribution shift and continual evaluation — highly relevant to zero-shot/few-shot forecasting, long-horizon robustness, and realistic evaluation methodology.

stories.title: Reassembling Distributed Risk: Trajectory-Conditioned Action Generation for Multi-Turn Agent Safety
stories.summary: ReDiR is a generation-time defense for tool-using LLM agents that conditions action generation on trajectory-level security evidence. It compresses the current trajectory into a compact latent safety representation before each action and injects this into the frozen base model, learned via same-model, cross-view supervision from an explicit task view to recover distributed safety evidence from multi-turn trajectories. Evaluations show ReDiR reduces attack success rates on two agent-safety benchmarks across three model families and eight held-out tool domains while preserving benign fidelity and maintaining low computational overhead.
stories.why_it_matters: Directly integrates cross-turn security signals into generation-time action synthesis, aligning with concerns about distributed risk in multi-turn tool use and reducing reliance on post-hoc or runtime-specific safety modules.
stories.reason: Directly targets multi-turn agentic attack surface where distributed malicious intent is hidden across actions—aligns tightly with LLM security, agent tool-use risk, and evaluation of long-horizon defenses; high relevance for designing red-teaming and runtime guardrails.

stories.title: Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection
stories.summary: The work addresses backdoor purification for LoRA-tuned LLMs without relying on triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining of suspect parameters. It proposes extracting high-fidelity backdoor directions and projecting LoRA updates onto orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels per layer/head, thereby purifying the model. Empirically, null-space projection reduces attack success rate from ~100% to <10% while preserving the base model's capabilities and the adapter’s downstream skills.
stories.why_it_matters: Directly targets backdoor mitigation in PEFT-enabled LLMs with no-retraining requirements, aligning with practical security controls for LoRA-tuned systems.
stories.reason: Directly addresses backdoor purification/removal in LLMs and LoRA/PEFT contexts, a core security topic with practical defense implications.

stories_overflow.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
stories_overflow.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

stories_overflow.title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
stories_overflow.summary: This work introduces SkillsMetric, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores LLM agent skills across pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch. Using an adversarial dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types and the SkillMD-138K corpus, it reports AUC 0.93 and 5-fold CV F1 73.4%±0.5%, with 93% detection for data exfiltration and steganographic payloads. It also exposes blind spots—0% detection for host destruction via common shell commands and 42% for prompt injection—arguing static analysis alone is insufficient and should be paired with semantic review in defense-in-depth.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly maps the detection boundary of static analysis for agent skills, highlighting failure modes (e.g., prompt injection, host destruction) that inform red-teaming, hybrid detection pipelines, and security benchmarks for LLM agents.
stories_overflow.reason: Static analysis scoring of agent 'skills' maps to supply-chain and capability-based attack surfaces for LLM agents and helps red-teaming/defense of tool-augmented systems.

stories_overflow.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
stories_overflow.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
stories_overflow.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

stories_overflow.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations, the method reveals systematic temporal shifts in influential data: literature-related data align more with the parameter trajectory early, while STEM data align more later. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across configurations, offering a tractable trajectory-level perspective that complements task-based influence analyses.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Gives a practical, retraining-free way to map which data sources steer pretraining trajectories over time, informing data curation, curriculum, and security-relevant provenance audits for LLMs.
stories_overflow.reason: Proposes a task-agnostic measure of individual-example influence during LM pretraining which is highly relevant to data provenance, extraction/attribution, contamination, and training-time attack/defense analysis.

stories_overflow.title: Proving the Utility of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity Simulations: A Comprehensive Examination
stories_overflow.summary: The paper evaluates LLMs for cybersecurity simulations, using YAML to represent complex network configurations and to drive pipelines that support RL agent training. It compares LLM-based techniques to classical methods like Double Q-learning with PER, claiming improved efficiency, adaptability, and realism in cyberattack simulations. In benchmarks on multiple synthetic topologies, LLM-instantiated Python agents reached up to a 94.5% compromise rate and 0.02–0.06s per assessment, a ~25,000x–50,000x speedup over traditional RL cycles.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Shows LLM-driven generation/execution pipelines can massively accelerate cyber-sim training and evaluation, relevant to secure LLM autonomy and sim-to-real robustness for time-series/agentic models.
stories_overflow.reason: Large-scale experimental evaluation of indirect prompt injection across channels and payloads maps closely to prompt-injection/jailbreak threat modeling and red-teaming methodology.

stories_overflow.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, data-free, model-internal signal for adversarial update filtering in federated LLM training, aligning with robustness and integrity concerns in LLM security.
stories_overflow.reason: FedLNS proposes a practical server-side defense against malicious client updates in federated LLM training—directly relevant to attack surfaces (poisoning, integrity) for deployed LLMs.

stories_overflow.title: Climbing the Hill: Prompt Injection Red-Teaming Against Frontier Models with Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
stories_overflow.summary: The work tackles prompt injection as a major security risk for LLMs and LLM-based agents by using RL-driven red-teaming to train attacker LLMs. It addresses the cold-start problem for frontier models (e.g., GPT-6-Luna) with curriculum learning, warming the attacker LLM through a sequence of increasingly robust targets and partial success at each stage. Empirical results show high ASR@10 against GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-5.6-Terra, outperforming RL-Hammer and PISmith, with demonstrated transferability of attacker LLMs across multiple frontier LLMs; code is released.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to frontier-model security and attacker transferability, informing curriculum-based red-teaming strategies for evaluating time-sensitive LLM defenses and agent safety in high-stakes settings.
stories_overflow.reason: Prominent LLM security focus (prompt injection, red-teaming, verifier integrity) with potential adversarial evaluation implications.

stories_overflow.title: Removing the NEEDLE in the Haystack: Backdoor Removal in LLMs via Weight Orthogonalisation
stories_overflow.summary: NEEDLE is a training-free method for targeted backdoor removal in LLMs that first identifies a backdoor trigger, then estimates a backdoor direction and a refusal subspace via activation vectors. It then applies sequential weight orthogonalisation to suppress the backdoor while preserving refusal-related representations, avoiding reliance on a clean reference model or original poisoned training data. Evaluated across model families and attack types, NEEDLE achieves the lowest mean Attack Success Rate among the defences, including 0% on code injection attacks, and induces the smallest KL divergence with minimal impacts on capability and safety.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Offers a training-free, targeted backdoor removal approach that preserves functional safety/capability, aligning with practical needs in LLM security and model integrity without requiring original poisoned data or clean references.
stories_overflow.reason: Proposes training-free backdoor removal (NEEDLE) with weight orthogonalisation, relevant to defense and robustness of LLMs.

stories_overflow.title: COPEX: Benchmarking LLM Robustness to Adversarial Context Across Model Context Protocol Layers
stories_overflow.summary: COPEX benchmarks LLM robustness to adversarial context across MCP layers by fixing the surrounding agent stack and varying only the tool-selecting model, isolating model susceptibility from guardrails and orchestration. It covers 25 attack types across 125 scenarios over four entry surfaces (model/agent, client, server/tool, transport) and evaluates nine models with 3,375 trials, reporting a mean attack success rate of 64.4% and surface means from 58.3% to 71.4%. The study shows that some client- and transport-level attacks can partly bypass model observation or control, and reports that combined input and context scanning reduces attack success by 49.6% on an eight-attack defense subset versus undefended; the benchmark is hosted at https://github.com/inspire-center/copex.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Provides a controlled, decomposition-style evaluation of adversarial context exposure across MCP layers, directly relevant for assessing model-level robustness separate from system orchestration and defense rails.
stories_overflow.reason: Directly targets adversarial robustness benchmarks for LLM-based MCP/security workflows, aligning with prompt/guardrail evaluation in LLM security.

stories_overflow.title: Do All LLMs Know When They're Being Harmful? A Reproducibility Study of Latent-Space Safety Probes Across Model Families
stories_overflow.summary: This study reproduces Khatri et al.’s pipeline for training lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations to detect harmful prompts, matching the original LLaMA-3.1-8B results within 0.37 F1 points (0.2 on BeaverTails). It extends the evaluation across Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2-7B on WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, and AEGIS 2.0, finding F1 within about one point of the LLaMA-3.1-8B values using the same probe architecture. It also assesses nondeterminism by varying seeds and reports that final token latent vectors were invariant to seed across architectures.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Suggests simple latent-space probes generalize across model families with stable activations, informing scalable, low-overhead safety detection for LLMs and complementing guardrail strategies.
stories_overflow.reason: Reproducibility of latent safety probes across model families evaluates a lightweight detection approach that could scale as a defense or monitoring tool for harmful prompt detection.

stories_overflow.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
stories_overflow.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
stories_overflow.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

stories_overflow.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces J-Access, an inference-time audit that projects intermediate representations into vocabulary space to measure how often target concepts remain accessible along the output pathway, hypothesizing that residual accessibility predicts recovery susceptibility. Auditing 398 public unlearned models across eight methods, they find most retain accessibility above a retain-only gold level, pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level (but not per-fact), and directly minimizing J-Access causes the model to hide knowledge from the audit while increasing post-attack recovery. They conclude J-Access is useful as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility and caution against turning internal audits into optimization targets without validation.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Offers an actionable, model-level risk signal for unlearning robustness and a clear warning about Goodharting internal audits—relevant for designing secure unlearning and audit pipelines in LLMs.
stories_overflow.reason: Investigates latent recovery after LLM unlearning with an audit (J‑Access) — important for data‑removal/extraction risk monitoring and evaluation methodology.

stories_overflow.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
stories_overflow.summary: The work frames judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem that, using a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, estimates target-relative roles: copies, complements, and specialists. These roles yield a policy to drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists on slices, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold, producing a reusable, auditable call plan. It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, auditable routing/early-stopping policy for multi-judge LLM evaluation that balances risk and cost across slices—directly relevant to secure deployment and panel design in LLM oversight and verifiers for time-series or reasoning tasks.
stories_overflow.reason: Optimizing which judges to call and when directly impacts scalable red-teaming, evaluation budgets, and LLM-as-judge pipelines relevant to security and agent verification.

stories_overflow.title: LLM-based Agents for Forecasting and Prediction: Methods, Training, Evaluation, and Applications
stories_overflow.summary: The paper surveys LLM-based forecasting agents, organizing architectures into standalone LLM workflows over temporal inputs, tool/retrieval-augmented agents, and hybrids with statistical or foundation models. It reviews training and evaluation practices and highlights negative evidence such as sensitivity to small perturbations, ablations showing no accuracy gains from the LLM, and potential benchmark contamination confounding temporal reasoning claims. Applications span finance, weather, health, energy, and operations, with the core limitation identified as measurement, motivating needs for robust calibration under shift, contamination-resistant live evaluation, explicit cost–accuracy reporting, and methods addressing forecast-induced feedback effects.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Concise map of architectures, pitfalls, and eval gaps for LLM-in-the-loop forecasting—useful for security-minded eval design, contamination control, calibration under shift, and coupling with time-series FMs.
stories_overflow.reason: Directly addresses LLM agents applied to forecasting/time-series, covers architectures (standalone, tool-augmented, hybrid) and evaluation — aligns strongly with time-series foundation models and agentic prediction use cases relevant to security/testing of forecasting agents.

stories_overflow.title: Calibrated Decision Models for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: JEV and Laya as System One Decision Layers for LLM-Driven Pentest Agents
stories_overflow.summary: The paper proposes using System One decision models—lightweight, non-generative classifiers that provide calibrated verdicts—to support autonomous pentest decision-making (finding adjudication, severity recalibration, agent pruning, and confirmation loops) in LLM-driven harnesses. It conducts an exploratory NeuroSploit case study comparing a run with TypeSafe System One (Jev) versus one without, using a web target with 13 vulnerabilities, and reports differences in severity distribution, runtime, and grading by exposed data type, noting that statistical significance is not established. It surveys specifications for Jev, Jev-Ultrafast, and Laya, discusses training approaches (RLHF, RLAIF, RLCD, RLHV) and their security implications, and proposes Rave, a domain-adapted System One model with an outlined training data, evaluation protocol, and potential impact on harness assurance.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It directly addresses calibrated, non-LLM decision layers to reduce false positives, wasted compute, and miscalibrated severity in LLM-driven pentest agents, with a concrete wiring of System One decisions to existing penetration-testing workflows.
stories_overflow.reason: Autonomous pentest agents involve LLM security, agent decision layers, and efficiency considerations in deployment.

stories_overflow.title: No Free Efficiency: Revisiting the Trade-off Between Training Efficiency and Model Vulnerability
stories_overflow.summary: Training efficiency strategies, including selective data sampling, efficient pre-training, and simplified RL pipelines, are explored for their impact on robustness. Across vision and language models, efficiency-oriented training is shown to increase susceptibility to adversarial and privacy attacks, with sharper loss geometry and systematic changes in internal representations. The study also analyzes zero RL training, finding greater catastrophic forgetting and overconfidence under simplified RL recipes, advocating for multi-objective training that balances performance, cost, and security.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly links efficiency gains to security/vulnerability concerns across domains, relevant to work on LLM security and time-series foundation models where efficiency-driven practices may affect robustness and privacy.
stories_overflow.reason: Prompt injection red-teaming with curriculum RL directly targets frontier-model security and robustness evaluation.

stories_overflow.title: From Experience to Expertise: Adoption-Aware Memory Learning for Data-Scarce NPU Kernel Synthesis
stories_overflow.summary: SAGE is a persistent self-improving agent for NPU kernel synthesis that addresses transfer gaps from LLMs by using memory-based learning with adoption-aware mechanisms. Adoption-Traced Utility estimation (ATU) combines explicit adoption records with kernel evaluation outcomes for credit assignment, while Utility-Gated Consolidation (UGC) uses positive utility and repeated adoption across operators to abstract reusable rules into a bounded resident context. On NPUKernelBench and with GLM-5.3, SAGE shows higher execution rates and faster sparse attention performance compared to baselines and torch_npu, indicating effective accumulation and reuse of hardware-specific knowledge across tasks.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Demonstrates adoption-aware credit assignment and selective consolidation to transfer hardware-specific knowledge across tasks, relevant to ML security and time-series LLMs working with DSAs and heterogeneous memory hierarchies.
stories_overflow.reason: Item 4/9 focuses on prompt injection and mechanistic understanding of LLM failure modes, aligning with LLM-security and evaluation of defenses.

stories_overflow.title: Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series
stories_overflow.summary: They use a large language model not as the detector but as the author of an autonomous loop that edits a compact NumPy program under a leakage-free objective, retaining the best-scoring detector found. The loop yields two compact detectors (one univariate, one multivariate) that describe short windows by local spectral features and compare to the training-region distribution via a covariance-aware distance. On the TSB-AD benchmark these detectors outperform classical, deep, and foundation-model baselines, train no networks, require no GPUs, and the multivariate detector is faster than comparable baselines; the approach demonstrates LLM-driven program search as a practical route to accurate, efficient, and transparent detectors.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Demonstrates practical, GPU-free, compact detectors driven by LLM-guided program search, aligning with goals for interpretable, efficient anomaly detection in time-series LLM-enabled research.
stories_overflow.reason: Autonomous discovery loop for compact, interpretable time-series detectors using LLMs; intersects TSFM with interpretability and evaluation.

stories_overflow.title: Jailbreaking Open-Weight LLMs via Random Embedding Perturbations
stories_overflow.summary: The paper exposes safety vulnerabilities in six open-weight LLMs of varying sizes, showing they can produce harmful or unsafe responses on the JailbreakBench benchmark. It introduces Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), a fast jailbreaking attack that adds independent Gaussian noise to prompt embedding vectors without gradient computations or internal weight changes. Repeatedly sampling additive noise yields unsafe responses, with first successful jailbreak typically within one minute, and PEV achieves unsafe outputs across all models for all prompts, outperforming prior methods in compute efficiency.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a lightweight, perturbation-based failure mode in open-weight LLM safety, highlighting a practical attack surface for embedding-space robustness and informing evaluation and defense strategies in LLM security and time-series foundation model contexts.
stories_overflow.reason: Jailbreaking open-weight LLMs via random embedding perturbations; directly about exploitation and defense of safety barriers.

stories_overflow.title: Threat-Preserving Representation Sensitivity in Agent-Security Benchmarks
stories_overflow.summary: Security benchmarks for LLM-based agents report ASR as a measure of robustness, assuming it reflects agent security. The paper introduces threat-preserving representation sensitivity (TPRS) to quantify how ASR changes when agent-visible representation changes while fixing task, harmful action, security policy, ground truth, environment, and evaluation criteria. Experiments show that substituting threat-related vs. neutral names in benchmarks can shift ASR by notable margins across ASB, MCPTox, and AgentDojo, and that token-compatible threat-neutral names reproduce much of the shift; overall, a single representation-dependent score may not generalize across threat-preserving representations, advocating performance evaluation over a controlled set of representations.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to evaluating robustness claims under representation shifts, a key concern for LLM security benchmarks and time-series foundation models where representation-sensitive attacks can mislead security assessments.
stories_overflow.reason: Examines how benchmark representations affect measured security of agent systems; relevant to benchmark validity in security tests.

stories_overflow.title: DataSense-Bench: The First Step Toward an AI Scientist
stories_overflow.summary: DataSense-Bench investigates whether frontier AI models can reliably select data for training by tackling data selection and performance forecasting in ML. The study allows AI agents to inspect data, generate/run analysis code, and execute model forward passes to choose and rank candidate training subsets, which are then used to fine-tune a small LLM and evaluated under a standardized protocol. The benchmark uses OpenThoughts-Agent and EnvScaler trajectories (TBLite and BFCL evaluations) to assess post-training performance of top-ranked subsets and ranking accuracy, reporting limited selection gains over random choice and inconsistent ranking across tasks, with agents often relying on similar data signals but interpreting training value differently.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to data-centric ML and AI system evaluation, linking data selection quality to post-training impact and ranking reliability in LLM fine-tuning scenarios.
stories_overflow.reason: Introduces a multivariate time-series foundation model with primitive-based pretraining—core to TSFM and generalization across domains.

stories_overflow.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
stories_overflow.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
stories_overflow.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

stories_overflow.title: Diversity Matters: Distributional Feature Coverage Sample Selection for Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces DFCS, a training-free, trigger-agnostic sample selection method that clusters pretrained features into one region per poisoning slot and picks centroid-nearest samples to avoid redundant poisons. A local first-order analysis links this allocation to feature-coverage and representative-mass terms. On CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and Imagenette with BadNets and Blended attacks, DFCS achieves the highest mean ASR among seven selectors in all six settings, averaging 96.30% and surpassing the strongest comparator by 4.60 points on average while maintaining clean accuracy.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It highlights a simple, training-free selection principle that boosts low-budget dirty-label backdoor potency, informing both attack design and defenses that rely on data diversity and feature coverage.
stories_overflow.reason: Data-efficient backdoor attack selection is directly relevant to poisoning threats against models and informs attack surface/defense design, though not LLM-specific and focused on vision-style feature clustering.

stories_overflow.title: ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions
stories_overflow.summary: ProbGuard reframes LLM safety assessment as probabilistic risk estimation over the model’s early output distribution rather than deterministic classification on completed token sequences. It estimates the probability of unsafe continuation via Monte Carlo over generated prefix distributions and calibrates this risk through post-training, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations. Empirically, it achieves the best calibration across nine model–dataset settings (average Brier and ECE reduced by 79.6% and 71.9% vs. the best baseline) and caps jailbreak attack success to ≤1% after only the first ten decoding steps.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It operationalizes distribution-aware, early-stage safety control with strong calibration—useful for red-teaming defenses, risk-sensitive deployment, and aligning with probabilistic guardrail research and time-series-style forecasting over generation trajectories.
stories_overflow.reason: Proposes a novel metric (feature nonlocality) to assess abstraction level of learned features from sparse autoencoders; useful for mechanistic interpretability and evaluating claims about high-level features relevant to jailbreak/mechanistic work.

stories_overflow.title: Probing the Prefill: Detecting Code Vulnerabilities via Latent Activations
stories_overflow.summary: The authors test whether LLM hidden states during prefill encode vulnerability signals when reading C/C++ code by extracting last prefill token activations from four models and training small MLP probes. Across four function-level benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul, Draper VDISC, PrimeVul), probes (13.4–16.0M params, <0.2% of base) reach 41.7% average F1, with a Qwen3.5-9B probe hitting 68.8% F1 on Devign, comparable to a fine-tuned-classifier SOTA (67.9%). Performance lags SOTA on the more imbalanced datasets, indicating partial but meaningful vulnerability information in frozen, general-purpose LLM activations and motivating model-native screening approaches.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Shows actionable signal for vulnerability detection resides in prefill activations, suggesting low-overhead, model-native monitors as an alternative or complement to post-hoc judges/classifiers.
stories_overflow.reason: Reproduction and sensitivity analysis of WEASEL 2.0 across UCR datasets is directly relevant to time-series benchmark validity and practical model choices (ensemble sizing).

stories_overflow.title: Do Time-Series Foundation Models Pay Off for Industrial Monitoring? A Cost-Aware Empirical Study
stories_overflow.summary: This study evaluates TSFMs versus lightweight baselines for industrial monitoring across three settings: C-MAPSS degradation risk, MIMII anomalous-sound detection with normal-only training, and BDG2 residual-diagnostics with synthetic perturbations. TCN-AE and OCSVM outperform MOMENT reconstruction on C-MAPSS and MIMII respectively, while TimesFM 2.5 yields the lowest forecast error and highest synthetic AUROC on the BDG2 panel with similar AUPRC to fitted residual models; MOMENT shows higher latency, VRAM, and state size than TCN-AE. Overall, under frozen zero-shot use, TSFMs provide task-dependent benefits rather than universally replacing compact fitted models.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It offers a cost-aware, protocol-matched comparison showing when zero-shot TSFMs beat fitted light baselines in industrial anomaly/diagnostics workflows, informing deployment choices for secure, resource-constrained monitoring systems.

stories_overflow.title: Poster: FedWM-Guard: Thwarting Imagination Poisoning in Federated World Model-based Autonomous Driving
stories_overflow.summary: Federated learning for world model–based autonomous driving enables training without sharing raw vehicle data but introduces a safety-critical integrity boundary in model aggregation. The paper defines imagination poisoning, where compromised clients submit bounded WM updates that preserve short-horizon predictions while corrupting long-horizon, trigger-conditioned rollouts during training, misleading downstream planners. FedWM-Guard is proposed as a defense that characterizes planner-facing rollouts, screens authenticated updates in hidden-canary scenarios, audits predicted futures against later observations, and triggers a WM-independent safety shield under persistent inconsistency, focusing on what updates make the model imagine rather than solely their parameter-space properties, with plans to evaluate under non-IID data, adaptive attacks, and benign distribution shifts.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It targets a novel threat surface in federated WM-AD that is directly relevant to LLM/security-oriented time-series RM/FD scenarios where planners rely on predictive rollouts.
stories_overflow.reason: Relates to LLM security via prompt injection and red-teaming; includes evaluation aspects relevant to security testing.

stories_overflow.title: DGF-Bench: A Benchmark for Simulating and Auditing Deception Against Multi-Agent Governance Boards
stories_overflow.summary: DGF-Bench is a benchmark where a board of agent gates evaluates synthetic dossiers against 61 executable rules, with 42 authoritative records and 32 narrative documents, while an attacker injects deceptive content into non-vouched evidence. Attacks do not alter authoritative values, so a dossier’s reference decisions remain the same as the clean copy; success is only counted when an agent takes the exact injected action prompted by the attack. Across 2,622 attacked gate runs, seven direct-order, false-data and false-authority attacks yielded one attributable success against five models, while task-aligned attacks mimicking the organization’s process bypassed four models; DGF scores ranged from 96.2 to 26.9, with some records-based attacks succeeding against multiple models; the package dgf-bench computes the DGF score with a single command.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Directly measures deception resilience of multi-agent governance-style pipelines under realistic, record-consistent attack injections relevant to LLM security and auditability.

stories_overflow.title: Quantifying Behavioral Tails in Black-Box Language Models
stories_overflow.summary: RareTrap introduces a framework for estimating the probability of severe behaviors in black box LLMs by using a surrogate LLM to create a geometry-aware mapping from a low-dimensional latent reference space into token embeddings, thereby inducing a tractable and reproducible input prompt distribution. A response-level performance function quantifies behavior severity, enabling sequential rare event simulation that focuses evaluations on progressively more severe behaviors while preserving the induced prompt distribution. Evaluations on 10 open-weight and two frontier models (GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6) show that RareTrap can induce severe resource consumption behaviors and compute their probability with as few as 200 evaluations, offering a principled approach for model developers to assess safety under a common distribution and prioritize alignment efforts.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Provides a principled, probability-grounded method to quantify rare, severe behaviors in black-box LLMs, relevant for time-series foundation models and security-focused ML research.

From these forecasts, it derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence and fuses multi-horizon signals to decide on interventions before tool executions. Across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive baselines with the best safety-utility trade-off and averages 25 ms end-to-end latency per call.

stories_overflow.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.

stories_overflow.title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces LabelFusion-TS, which combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and an ensemble of time-series transformers over pre-publication market series via a small voting network to classify FOMC sentences as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Due to limited human labels (~1k sentences), the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on LLM-generated weak labels and then fine-tuned on human annotations. Trained on data up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015–2022, the fused system attains 70.2% weighted F1, surpassing a zero-shot LLM at 64.1% and overtaking it with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences.

stories_overflow.summary: This work reconstructs a 500-cell federated aggregation benchmark across five methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets), recovering 454 original runs and 36 repairs/reruns, with 10 SVHN cells covered only by summary provenance. Trimmed Mean has the best clean macro-mean accuracy and lowest mean within-task rank, while Krum shows the top recorded accuracy under sign-flipping and Gaussian, and these rankings persist when restricted to fully logged task pairs. Audits reveal the BadNets metric is actually TTLR (all test inputs triggered) and a FedPARETO pathway where reported predictive summaries may not match the corrupted updates used for aggregation, so results are descriptive within recorded configs rather than universal robustness claims.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Highlights reproducibility gaps, metric mis-specification (TTLR), and aggregation/provenance pitfalls that can confound robustness claims in federated settings relevant to secure FL and poisoning/backdoor evaluation.

stories_overflow.title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces ORBIT, a training paradigm for TSFMs that explicitly controls pre-training distributions via Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling and Omni-Range Incremental Training. It trains Falcon-2.0, a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, under this regime. The authors also propose Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment to align shallow and deep representations, and report strong zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench across diverse domains and frequencies.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: It provides a principled, controllable pretraining regime and lightweight representation alignment that could transfer to secure LLM pretraining curricula and to robust TSFM deployment across heterogeneous, imbalanced time-series corpora.

Under forward-in-time, CVE-disjoint evaluation, it significantly outperforms CVSS, EPSS, and rule-based evidence fusion, surfacing 80.0% of future KEV CVEs in the top 20 and 95.9% in the top 50 on a held-out test split. Early-warning analysis shows it flags a substantial fraction of later KEV entries before catalog inclusion, enabling timely, evidence-grounded triage.

stories_overflow.summary: The paper introduces IoTVulBench, a human-verified, contamination-screened benchmark for cross-corpus IoT firmware vulnerability detection, and evaluates five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies with ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Models trained on IoTVulBench outperform matched single-source datasets (MCC 0.58 vs. 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A), with staged curriculum learning raising MCC to 0.69 and a diversity-optimized ensemble reaching 0.73, surpassing a static analyzer (0.31) and PrimeVul by large margins while maintaining 86% performance under identifier renaming and showing strong calibration and largely faithful explanations. At a 0.5% FPR, the model missed 21% of vulnerabilities versus 71% for the strongest comparator, indicating domain-matched data and curriculum design—not model scale alone—drive generalization in firmware vulnerability detection.

It delivers substantial gains for the Writer Agent and compares favorably on public benchmarks, achieving the top BFCL Core score of 0.785 and the highest six-benchmark mean among its cohort. The model is also competitive or leading in the authors’ bias and safety evaluations relative to comparators.
stories_overflow.why_it_matters: Tight, KL-anchored post-training on compact synthetic tool-use traces yielding SOTA-ish agentic performance is directly relevant to secure tool-use alignment and data-efficient post-training strategies for robust, controllable agents.

stories_overflow.title: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
stories_overflow.summary: The paper audits temporal leakage in financial-news direction prediction across 49,799 articles and 16 model–feature setups (TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, fine-tuned RoBERTa-large/DeBERTa-v3-large, and Llama-3/Qwen2.5 zero/few-shot and LoRA), finding random splits inflate MCC by 1.1×–6.5×, increasing with capacity and feature richness, and that end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning further amplifies the gap (size-matched ratio 1.75×). Under near-chronological evaluation, only M&A shows a positive locked-test signal (TF-IDF MCC 0.138 train-only, 0.068 after train∪val refit; 10,000-permutation p < 10^{-3}), which does not transfer to FNSPID 2009–2020 U.S. data, suggesting localization to 2024–2025 European-tilted M&A semantics. Three role labelers indicate acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, and the authors argue chronological splits purge stale, predictable components, leaving a small, event-localized, lexically shallow residual and call for mandatory leakage audits in financial NLP benchmarks.

items.title: From Runnable to Verifiable: An Independent Reproducibility Study of LLM/Agent-Driven Vulnerability Validation Artifacts
items.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
items.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.

items.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
items.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
items.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
items.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

items.title: Security Assessment of DeepSeek Harness with A.I.G: Evaluating Resistance to Indirect Prompt Injection
items.summary: This work evaluates indirect prompt injection against DeepSeek Harness using AI-Infra-Guard to generate tests, deliver controlled taint across 16 channels and two carrier modes, run 14,560 executions, and analyze traces with both rule-based and LLM-based judges. The strongest observed attack success rates are 17.0% under LLMJudge for a fake-completion attack (text), 25.5% under RuleJudge for hidden Unicode (file), and 16.0% under RuleJudge for the skills channel (file), with LLMJudge assigning more partial compliance than RuleJudge (7.3% vs. 2.0%). The study connects outcomes to DSH’s handling of tool results, extra contexts, and tool-call policy hooks, and proposes controls between untrusted content and sensitive actions, with code released at the linked repository.
items.why_it_matters: Provides a large-scale, reproducible, channel- and payload-stratified benchmark of indirect prompt injection on an agentic LLM stack with dual judges, informing defense design and evaluation baselines.
items.reason: Black-box auditing of vendor-hosted LLM APIs via statistical repeated-query testing is highly relevant for red-teaming, API threat models, and evaluation methodology.

items.title: Reassembling Distributed Risk: Trajectory-Conditioned Action Generation for Multi-Turn Agent Safety
items.summary: ReDiR is a generation-time defense for tool-using LLM agents that conditions action generation on trajectory-level security evidence. It compresses the current trajectory into a compact latent safety representation before each action and injects this into the frozen base model, learned via same-model, cross-view supervision from an explicit task view to recover distributed safety evidence from multi-turn trajectories. Evaluations show ReDiR reduces attack success rates on two agent-safety benchmarks across three model families and eight held-out tool domains while preserving benign fidelity and maintaining low computational overhead.
items.why_it_matters: Directly integrates cross-turn security signals into generation-time action synthesis, aligning with concerns about distributed risk in multi-turn tool use and reducing reliance on post-hoc or runtime-specific safety modules.
items.reason: Directly targets multi-turn agentic attack surface where distributed malicious intent is hidden across actions—aligns tightly with LLM security, agent tool-use risk, and evaluation of long-horizon defenses; high relevance for designing red-teaming and runtime guardrails.

items.title: Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection
items.summary: The work addresses backdoor purification for LoRA-tuned LLMs without relying on triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining of suspect parameters. items.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding

items.title: Security Assessment of DeepSeek Harness with A.I.G: Evaluating Resistance to Indirect Prompt Injection
items.summary: This work evaluates indirect prompt injection against DeepSeek Harness using AI-Infra-Guard to generate tests, deliver controlled taint across 16 channels and two carrier modes, run 14,560 executions, and analyze traces with both rule-based and LLM-based judges. The strongest observed attack success rates are 17.0% under LLMJudge for a fake-completion attack (text), 25.5% under RuleJudge for hidden Unicode (file), and 16.0% under RuleJudge for the skills channel (file), with LLMJudge assigning more partial compliance than RuleJudge (7.3% vs. 2.0%). The study connects outcomes to DSH’s handling of tool results, extra contexts, and tool-call policy hooks, and proposes controls between untrusted content and sensitive actions, with code released at the linked repository.
items.why_it_matters: Provides a large-scale, reproducible, channel- and payload-stratified benchmark of indirect prompt injection on an agentic LLM stack with dual judges, informing defense design and evaluation baselines.

items.title: COPEX: Benchmarking LLM Robustness to Adversarial Context Across Model Context Protocol Layers
items.summary: COPEX benchmarks LLM robustness to adversarial context across MCP layers by fixing the surrounding agent stack and varying only the tool-selecting model, isolating model susceptibility from guardrails and orchestration. It covers 25 attack types across 125 scenarios over four entry surfaces (model/agent, client, server/tool, transport) and evaluates nine models with 3,375 trials, reporting a mean attack success rate of 64.4% and surface means from 58.3% to 71.4%. The study shows that some client- and transport-level attacks can partly bypass model observation or control, and reports that combined input and context scanning reduces attack success by 49.6% on an eight-attack defense subset versus undefended; the benchmark is hosted at https://github.com/inspire-center/copex.

items.title: DGF-Bench: A Benchmark for Simulating and Auditing Deception Against Multi-Agent Governance Boards
items.summary: DGF-Bench is a benchmark where a board of agent gates evaluates synthetic dossiers against 61 executable rules, with 42 authoritative records and 32 narrative documents, while an attacker injects deceptive content into non-vouched evidence. Attacks do not alter authoritative values, so a dossier’s reference decisions remain the same as the clean copy; success is only counted when an agent takes the exact injected action prompted by the attack. Across 2,622 attacked gate runs, seven direct-order, false-data and false-authority attacks yielded one attributable success against five models, while task-aligned attacks mimicking the organization’s process bypassed four models; DGF scores ranged from 96.2 to 26.9, with some records-based attacks succeeding against multiple models; the package dgf-bench computes the DGF score with a single command.

llm-security.title: Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection
llm-security.summary: The work addresses backdoor purification for LoRA-tuned LLMs without relying on triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining of suspect parameters. It proposes extracting high-fidelity backdoor directions and projecting LoRA updates onto orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels per layer/head, thereby purifying the model. Empirically, null-space projection reduces attack success rate from ~100% to <10% while preserving the base model's capabilities and the adapter’s downstream skills.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly targets backdoor mitigation in PEFT-enabled LLMs with no-retraining requirements, aligning with practical security controls for LoRA-tuned systems.
llm-security.reason: Directly addresses backdoor purification/removal in LLMs and LoRA/PEFT contexts, a core security topic with practical defense implications.

llm-security.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
llm-security.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

llm-security.title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
llm-security.summary: This work introduces SkillsMetric, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores LLM agent skills across pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch. Using an adversarial dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types and the SkillMD-138K corpus, it reports AUC 0.93 and 5-fold CV F1 73.4%±0.5%, with 93% detection for data exfiltration and steganographic payloads. It also exposes blind spots—0% detection for host destruction via common shell commands and 42% for prompt injection—arguing static analysis alone is insufficient and should be paired with semantic review in defense-in-depth.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly maps the detection boundary of static analysis for agent skills, highlighting failure modes (e.g., prompt injection, host destruction) that inform red-teaming, hybrid detection pipelines, and security benchmarks for LLM agents.
llm-security.reason: Static analysis scoring of agent 'skills' maps to supply-chain and capability-based attack surfaces for LLM agents and helps red-teaming/defense of tool-augmented systems.

llm-security.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
llm-security.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
llm-security.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

llm-security.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations, the method reveals systematic temporal shifts in influential data: literature-related data align more with the parameter trajectory early, while STEM data align more later. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across configurations, offering a tractable trajectory-level perspective that complements task-based influence analyses.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Gives a practical, retraining-free way to map which data sources steer pretraining trajectories over time, informing data curation, curriculum, and security-relevant provenance audits for LLMs.
llm-security.reason: Proposes a task-agnostic measure of individual-example influence during LM pretraining which is highly relevant to data provenance, extraction/attribution, contamination, and training-time attack/defense analysis.

llm-security.title: Proving the Utility of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity Simulations: A Comprehensive Examination
llm-security.summary: The paper evaluates LLMs for cybersecurity simulations, using YAML to represent complex network configurations and to drive pipelines that support RL agent training. It compares LLM-based techniques to classical methods like Double Q-learning with PER, claiming improved efficiency, adaptability, and realism in cyberattack simulations. In benchmarks on multiple synthetic topologies, LLM-instantiated Python agents reached up to a 94.5% compromise rate and 0.02–0.06s per assessment, a ~25,000x–50,000x speedup over traditional RL cycles.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Shows LLM-driven generation/execution pipelines can massively accelerate cyber-sim training and evaluation, relevant to secure LLM autonomy and sim-to-real robustness for time-series/agentic models.
llm-security.reason: Large-scale experimental evaluation of indirect prompt injection across channels and payloads maps closely to prompt-injection/jailbreak threat modeling and red-teaming methodology.

llm-security.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, data-free, model-internal signal for adversarial update filtering in federated LLM training, aligning with robustness and integrity concerns in LLM security.
llm-security.reason: FedLNS proposes a practical server-side defense against malicious client updates in federated LLM training—directly relevant to attack surfaces (poisoning, integrity) for deployed LLMs.

llm-security.title: Climbing the Hill: Prompt Injection Red-Teaming Against Frontier Models with Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
llm-security.summary: The work tackles prompt injection as a major security risk for LLMs and LLM-based agents by using RL-driven red-teaming to train attacker LLMs. It addresses the cold-start problem for frontier models (e.g., GPT-6-Luna) with curriculum learning, warming the attacker LLM through a sequence of increasingly robust targets and partial success at each stage. Empirical results show high ASR@10 against GPT-5.6-Luna and GPT-5.6-Terra, outperforming RL-Hammer and PISmith, with demonstrated transferability of attacker LLMs across multiple frontier LLMs; code is released.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to frontier-model security and attacker transferability, informing curriculum-based red-teaming strategies for evaluating time-sensitive LLM defenses and agent safety in high-stakes settings.
llm-security.reason: Prominent LLM security focus (prompt injection, red-teaming, verifier integrity) with potential adversarial evaluation implications.

llm-security.title: Removing the NEEDLE in the Haystack: Backdoor Removal in LLMs via Weight Orthogonalisation
llm-security.summary: NEEDLE is a training-free method for targeted backdoor removal in LLMs that first identifies a backdoor trigger, then estimates a backdoor direction and a refusal subspace via activation vectors. It then applies sequential weight orthogonalisation to suppress the backdoor while preserving refusal-related representations, avoiding reliance on a clean reference model or original poisoned training data. Evaluated across model families and attack types, NEEDLE achieves the lowest mean Attack Success Rate among the defences, including 0% on code injection attacks, and induces the smallest KL divergence with minimal impacts on capability and safety.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a training-free, targeted backdoor removal approach that preserves functional safety/capability, aligning with practical needs in LLM security and model integrity without requiring original poisoned data or clean references.
llm-security.reason: Proposes training-free backdoor removal (NEEDLE) with weight orthogonalisation, relevant to defense and robustness of LLMs.
