llm-security.title: Do All LLMs Know When They're Being Harmful? A Reproducibility Study of Latent-Space Safety Probes Across Model Families
llm-security.summary: This study reproduces Khatri et al.’s pipeline for training lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations to detect harmful prompts, matching the original LLaMA-3.1-8B results within 0.37 F1 points (0.2 on BeaverTails). It extends the evaluation across Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2-7B on WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, and AEGIS 2.0, finding F1 within about one point of the LLaMA-3.1-8B values using the same probe architecture. It also assesses nondeterminism by varying seeds and reports that final token latent vectors were invariant to seed across architectures.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Suggests simple latent-space probes generalize across model families with stable activations, informing scalable, low-overhead safety detection for LLMs and complementing guardrail strategies.
llm-security.reason: Reproducibility of latent safety probes across model families evaluates a lightweight detection approach that could scale as a defense or monitoring tool for harmful prompt detection.

llm-security.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
llm-security.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
llm-security.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

llm-security.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces J-Access, an inference-time audit that projects intermediate representations into vocabulary space to measure how often target concepts remain accessible along the output pathway, hypothesizing that residual accessibility predicts recovery susceptibility. Auditing 398 public unlearned models across eight methods, they find most retain accessibility above a retain-only gold level, pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level (but not per-fact), and directly minimizing J-Access causes the model to hide knowledge from the audit while increasing post-attack recovery. They conclude J-Access is useful as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility and caution against turning internal audits into optimization targets without validation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers an actionable, model-level risk signal for unlearning robustness and a clear warning about Goodharting internal audits—relevant for designing secure unlearning and audit pipelines in LLMs.
llm-security.reason: Investigates latent recovery after LLM unlearning with an audit (J‑Access) — important for data‑removal/extraction risk monitoring and evaluation methodology.

llm-security.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
llm-security.summary: The work frames judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem that, using a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, estimates target-relative roles: copies, complements, and specialists. These roles yield a policy to drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists on slices, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold, producing a reusable, auditable call plan. It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, auditable routing/early-stopping policy for multi-judge LLM evaluation that balances risk and cost across slices—directly relevant to secure deployment and panel design in LLM oversight and verifiers for time-series or reasoning tasks.
llm-security.reason: Optimizing which judges to call and when directly impacts scalable red-teaming, evaluation budgets, and LLM-as-judge pipelines relevant to security and agent verification.

llm-security.title: Calibrated Decision Models for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: JEV and Laya as System One Decision Layers for LLM-Driven Pentest Agents
llm-security.summary: The paper proposes using System One decision models—lightweight, non-generative classifiers that provide calibrated verdicts—to support autonomous pentest decision-making (finding adjudication, severity recalibration, agent pruning, and confirmation loops) in LLM-driven harnesses. It conducts an exploratory NeuroSploit case study comparing a run with TypeSafe System One (Jev) versus one without, using a web target with 13 vulnerabilities, and reports differences in severity distribution, runtime, and grading by exposed data type, noting that statistical significance is not established. It surveys specifications for Jev, Jev-Ultrafast, and Laya, discusses training approaches (RLHF, RLAIF, RLCD, RLHV) and their security implications, and proposes Rave, a domain-adapted System One model with an outlined training data, evaluation protocol, and potential impact on harness assurance.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It directly addresses calibrated, non-LLM decision layers to reduce false positives, wasted compute, and miscalibrated severity in LLM-driven pentest agents, with a concrete wiring of System One decisions to existing penetration-testing workflows.
llm-security.reason: Autonomous pentest agents involve LLM security, agent decision layers, and efficiency considerations in deployment.

llm-security.title: No Free Efficiency: Revisiting the Trade-off Between Training Efficiency and Model Vulnerability
llm-security.summary: Training efficiency strategies, including selective data sampling, efficient pre-training, and simplified RL pipelines, are explored for their impact on robustness. Across vision and language models, efficiency-oriented training is shown to increase susceptibility to adversarial and privacy attacks, with sharper loss geometry and systematic changes in internal representations. The study also analyzes zero RL training, finding greater catastrophic forgetting and overconfidence under simplified RL recipes, advocating for multi-objective training that balances performance, cost, and security.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly links efficiency gains to security/vulnerability concerns across domains, relevant to work on LLM security and time-series foundation models where efficiency-driven practices may affect robustness and privacy.
llm-security.reason: Prompt injection red-teaming with curriculum RL directly targets frontier-model security and robustness evaluation.

llm-security.title: From Experience to Expertise: Adoption-Aware Memory Learning for Data-Scarce NPU Kernel Synthesis
llm-security.summary: SAGE is a persistent self-improving agent for NPU kernel synthesis that addresses transfer gaps from LLMs by using memory-based learning with adoption-aware mechanisms. Adoption-Traced Utility estimation (ATU) combines explicit adoption records with kernel evaluation outcomes for credit assignment, while Utility-Gated Consolidation (UGC) uses positive utility and repeated adoption across operators to abstract reusable rules into a bounded resident context. On NPUKernelBench and with GLM-5.3, SAGE shows higher execution rates and faster sparse attention performance compared to baselines and torch_npu, indicating effective accumulation and reuse of hardware-specific knowledge across tasks.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Demonstrates adoption-aware credit assignment and selective consolidation to transfer hardware-specific knowledge across tasks, relevant to ML security and time-series LLMs working with DSAs and heterogeneous memory hierarchies.
llm-security.reason: Item 4/9 focuses on prompt injection and mechanistic understanding of LLM failure modes, aligning with LLM-security and evaluation of defenses.

llm-security.title: Jailbreaking Open-Weight LLMs via Random Embedding Perturbations
llm-security.summary: The paper exposes safety vulnerabilities in six open-weight LLMs of varying sizes, showing they can produce harmful or unsafe responses on the JailbreakBench benchmark. It introduces Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), a fast jailbreaking attack that adds independent Gaussian noise to prompt embedding vectors without gradient computations or internal weight changes. Repeatedly sampling additive noise yields unsafe responses, with first successful jailbreak typically within one minute, and PEV achieves unsafe outputs across all models for all prompts, outperforming prior methods in compute efficiency.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a lightweight, perturbation-based failure mode in open-weight LLM safety, highlighting a practical attack surface for embedding-space robustness and informing evaluation and defense strategies in LLM security and time-series foundation model contexts.
llm-security.reason: Jailbreaking open-weight LLMs via random embedding perturbations; directly about exploitation and defense of safety barriers.

llm-security.title: Threat-Preserving Representation Sensitivity in Agent-Security Benchmarks
llm-security.summary: Security benchmarks for LLM-based agents report ASR as a measure of robustness, assuming it reflects agent security. The paper introduces threat-preserving representation sensitivity (TPRS) to quantify how ASR changes when agent-visible representation changes while fixing task, harmful action, security policy, ground truth, environment, and evaluation criteria. Experiments show that substituting threat-related vs. neutral names in benchmarks can shift ASR by notable margins across ASB, MCPTox, and AgentDojo, and that token-compatible threat-neutral names reproduce much of the shift; overall, a single representation-dependent score may not generalize across threat-preserving representations, advocating performance evaluation over a controlled set of representations.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to evaluating robustness claims under representation shifts, a key concern for LLM security benchmarks and time-series foundation models where representation-sensitive attacks can mislead security assessments.
llm-security.reason: Examines how benchmark representations affect measured security of agent systems; relevant to benchmark validity in security tests.

llm-security.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
llm-security.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
llm-security.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

llm-security.title: Diversity Matters: Distributional Feature Coverage Sample Selection for Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces DFCS, a training-free, trigger-agnostic sample selection method that clusters pretrained features into one region per poisoning slot and picks centroid-nearest samples to avoid redundant poisons. A local first-order analysis links this allocation to feature-coverage and representative-mass terms. On CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and Imagenette with BadNets and Blended attacks, DFCS achieves the highest mean ASR among seven selectors in all six settings, averaging 96.30% and surpassing the strongest comparator by 4.60 points on average while maintaining clean accuracy.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It highlights a simple, training-free selection principle that boosts low-budget dirty-label backdoor potency, informing both attack design and defenses that rely on data diversity and feature coverage.
llm-security.reason: Data-efficient backdoor attack selection is directly relevant to poisoning threats against models and informs attack surface/defense design, though not LLM-specific and focused on vision-style feature clustering.

llm-security.title: Poster: FedWM-Guard: Thwarting Imagination Poisoning in Federated World Model-based Autonomous Driving
llm-security.summary: Federated learning for world model–based autonomous driving enables training without sharing raw vehicle data but introduces a safety-critical integrity boundary in model aggregation. The paper defines imagination poisoning, where compromised clients submit bounded WM updates that preserve short-horizon predictions while corrupting long-horizon, trigger-conditioned rollouts during training, misleading downstream planners. FedWM-Guard is proposed as a defense that characterizes planner-facing rollouts, screens authenticated updates in hidden-canary scenarios, audits predicted futures against later observations, and triggers a WM-independent safety shield under persistent inconsistency, focusing on what updates make the model imagine rather than solely their parameter-space properties, with plans to evaluate under non-IID data, adaptive attacks, and benign distribution shifts.

llm-security.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. Experiments on simulations and real-world shifts (DomainNet/VisDA and MIMIC-IV-Notes ICU mortality) show it matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains when no single baseline is reliable across the shifts considered.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.

llm-security.title: ThreatLens: Evidence-Guided Ranking of High-Priority CVEs
llm-security.summary: ThreatLens is a deployment-realistic CVE prioritization framework that ranks at review time using only cutoff-valid evidence and learns exploitation relevance from future CISA KEV entries as weak supervision. Under forward-in-time, CVE-disjoint evaluation, it significantly outperforms CVSS, EPSS, and rule-based evidence fusion, surfacing 80.0% of future KEV CVEs in the top 20 and 95.9% in the top 50 on a held-out test split. agents.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
agents.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.

agents.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
agents.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
agents.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

agents.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels

It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.

agents.title: Calibrated Decision Models for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: JEV and Laya as System One Decision Layers for LLM-Driven Pentest Agents

agents.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
agents.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. agents.title: Do Time-Series Foundation Models Pay Off for Industrial Monitoring? A Cost-Aware Empirical Study

evaluation.title: Reassembling Distributed Risk: Trajectory-Conditioned Action Generation for Multi-Turn Agent Safety
evaluation.summary: ReDiR is a generation-time defense for tool-using LLM agents that conditions action generation on trajectory-level security evidence. It compresses the current trajectory into a compact latent safety representation before each action and injects this into the frozen base model, learned via same-model, cross-view supervision from an explicit task view to recover distributed safety evidence from multi-turn trajectories. Evaluations show ReDiR reduces attack success rates on two agent-safety benchmarks across three model families and eight held-out tool domains while preserving benign fidelity and maintaining low computational overhead.

evaluation.title: Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection
evaluation.summary: The work addresses backdoor purification for LoRA-tuned LLMs without relying on triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining of suspect parameters. It proposes extracting high-fidelity backdoor directions and projecting LoRA updates onto orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels per layer/head, thereby purifying the model. Empirically, null-space projection reduces attack success rate from ~100% to <10% while preserving the base model's capabilities and the adapter’s downstream skills.

evaluation.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.

evaluation.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. evaluation.title: Climbing the Hill: Prompt Injection Red-Teaming Against Frontier Models with Curriculum Reinforcement Learning

evaluation.title: COPEX: Benchmarking LLM Robustness to Adversarial Context Across Model Context Protocol Layers
evaluation.summary: COPEX benchmarks LLM robustness to adversarial context across MCP layers by fixing the surrounding agent stack and varying only the tool-selecting model, isolating model susceptibility from guardrails and orchestration. It covers 25 attack types across 125 scenarios over four entry surfaces (model/agent, client, server/tool, transport) and evaluates nine models with 3,375 trials, reporting a mean attack success rate of 64.4% and surface means from 58.3% to 71.4%. The study shows that some client- and transport-level attacks can partly bypass model observation or control, and reports that combined input and context scanning reduces attack success by 49.6% on an eight-attack defense subset versus undefended; the benchmark is hosted at https://github.com/inspire-center/copex.

evaluation.title: From Experience to Expertise: Adoption-Aware Memory Learning for Data-Scarce NPU Kernel Synthesis
evaluation.summary: SAGE is a persistent self-improving agent for NPU kernel synthesis that addresses transfer gaps from LLMs by using memory-based learning with adoption-aware mechanisms. Adoption-Traced Utility estimation (ATU) combines explicit adoption records with kernel evaluation outcomes for credit assignment, while Utility-Gated Consolidation (UGC) uses positive utility and repeated adoption across operators to abstract reusable rules into a bounded resident context. On NPUKernelBench and with GLM-5.3, SAGE shows higher execution rates and faster sparse attention performance compared to baselines and torch_npu, indicating effective accumulation and reuse of hardware-specific knowledge across tasks.

evaluation.title: Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series
evaluation.summary: They use a large language model not as the detector but as the author of an autonomous loop that edits a compact NumPy program under a leakage-free objective, retaining the best-scoring detector found. The loop yields two compact detectors (one univariate, one multivariate) that describe short windows by local spectral features and compare to the training-region distribution via a covariance-aware distance. On the TSB-AD benchmark these detectors outperform classical, deep, and foundation-model baselines, train no networks, require no GPUs, and the multivariate detector is faster than comparable baselines; the approach demonstrates LLM-driven program search as a practical route to accurate, efficient, and transparent detectors.

evaluation.title: Jailbreaking Open-Weight LLMs via Random Embedding Perturbations
evaluation.summary: The paper exposes safety vulnerabilities in six open-weight LLMs of varying sizes, showing they can produce harmful or unsafe responses on the JailbreakBench benchmark. It introduces Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), a fast jailbreaking attack that adds independent Gaussian noise to prompt embedding vectors without gradient computations or internal weight changes. Repeatedly sampling additive noise yields unsafe responses, with first successful jailbreak typically within one minute, and PEV achieves unsafe outputs across all models for all prompts, outperforming prior methods in compute efficiency.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a lightweight, perturbation-based failure mode in open-weight LLM safety, highlighting a practical attack surface for embedding-space robustness and informing evaluation and defense strategies in LLM security and time-series foundation model contexts.

evaluation.title: Threat-Preserving Representation Sensitivity in Agent-Security Benchmarks
evaluation.summary: Security benchmarks for LLM-based agents report ASR as a measure of robustness, assuming it reflects agent security. The paper introduces threat-preserving representation sensitivity (TPRS) to quantify how ASR changes when agent-visible representation changes while fixing task, harmful action, security policy, ground truth, environment, and evaluation criteria. Experiments show that substituting threat-related vs. neutral names in benchmarks can shift ASR by notable margins across ASB, MCPTox, and AgentDojo, and that token-compatible threat-neutral names reproduce much of the shift; overall, a single representation-dependent score may not generalize across threat-preserving representations, advocating performance evaluation over a controlled set of representations.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to evaluating robustness claims under representation shifts, a key concern for LLM security benchmarks and time-series foundation models where representation-sensitive attacks can mislead security assessments.
evaluation.reason: Examines how benchmark representations affect measured security of agent systems; relevant to benchmark validity in security tests.

evaluation.title: ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions
evaluation.summary: ProbGuard reframes LLM safety assessment as probabilistic risk estimation over the model’s early output distribution rather than deterministic classification on completed token sequences. It estimates the probability of unsafe continuation via Monte Carlo over generated prefix distributions and calibrates this risk through post-training, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations. Empirically, it achieves the best calibration across nine model–dataset settings (average Brier and ECE reduced by 79.6% and 71.9% vs. the best baseline) and caps jailbreak attack success to ≤1% after only the first ten decoding steps.

evaluation.title: Probing the Prefill: Detecting Code Vulnerabilities via Latent Activations
evaluation.summary: The authors test whether LLM hidden states during prefill encode vulnerability signals when reading C/C++ code by extracting last prefill token activations from four models and training small MLP probes. Across four function-level benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul, Draper VDISC, PrimeVul), probes (13.4–16.0M params, <0.2% of base) reach 41.7% average F1, with a Qwen3.5-9B probe hitting 68.8% F1 on Devign, comparable to a fine-tuned-classifier SOTA (67.9%). Performance lags SOTA on the more imbalanced datasets, indicating partial but meaningful vulnerability information in frozen, general-purpose LLM activations and motivating model-native screening approaches.

evaluation.title: Do Time-Series Foundation Models Pay Off for Industrial Monitoring? A Cost-Aware Empirical Study
evaluation.summary: This study evaluates TSFMs versus lightweight baselines for industrial monitoring across three settings: C-MAPSS degradation risk, MIMII anomalous-sound detection with normal-only training, and BDG2 residual-diagnostics with synthetic perturbations. TCN-AE and OCSVM outperform MOMENT reconstruction on C-MAPSS and MIMII respectively, while TimesFM 2.5 yields the lowest forecast error and highest synthetic AUROC on the BDG2 panel with similar AUPRC to fitted residual models; MOMENT shows higher latency, VRAM, and state size than TCN-AE. Overall, under frozen zero-shot use, TSFMs provide task-dependent benefits rather than universally replacing compact fitted models.

evaluation.title: Poster: FedWM-Guard: Thwarting Imagination Poisoning in Federated World Model-based Autonomous Driving
evaluation.summary: Federated learning for world model–based autonomous driving enables training without sharing raw vehicle data but introduces a safety-critical integrity boundary in model aggregation. evaluation.title: Quantifying Behavioral Tails in Black-Box Language Models
evaluation.summary: RareTrap introduces a framework for estimating the probability of severe behaviors in black box LLMs by using a surrogate LLM to create a geometry-aware mapping from a low-dimensional latent reference space into token embeddings, thereby inducing a tractable and reproducible input prompt distribution. A response-level performance function quantifies behavior severity, enabling sequential rare event simulation that focuses evaluations on progressively more severe behaviors while preserving the induced prompt distribution. Evaluations on 10 open-weight and two frontier models (GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6) show that RareTrap can induce severe resource consumption behaviors and compute their probability with as few as 200 evaluations, offering a principled approach for model developers to assess safety under a common distribution and prioritize alignment efforts.

evaluation.title: Analysis of Federated Aggregation under Model Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks: A Reconstructed Cross-Dataset and Cross-Architecture Benchmark
evaluation.summary: This work reconstructs a 500-cell federated aggregation benchmark across five methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets), recovering 454 original runs and 36 repairs/reruns, with 10 SVHN cells covered only by summary provenance. evaluation.title: ThreatLens: Evidence-Guided Ranking of High-Priority CVEs

evaluation.title: Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Generalizable Vulnerability Detection in IoT Firmware
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces IoTVulBench, a human-verified, contamination-screened benchmark for cross-corpus IoT firmware vulnerability detection, and evaluates five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies with ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Models trained on IoTVulBench outperform matched single-source datasets (MCC 0.58 vs. 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A), with staged curriculum learning raising MCC to 0.69 and a diversity-optimized ensemble reaching 0.73, surpassing a static analyzer (0.31) and PrimeVul by large margins while maintaining 86% performance under identifier renaming and showing strong calibration and largely faithful explanations. At a 0.5% FPR, the model missed 21% of vulnerabilities versus 71% for the strongest comparator, indicating domain-matched data and curriculum design—not model scale alone—drive generalization in firmware vulnerability detection.

evaluation.title: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
evaluation.summary: The paper audits temporal leakage in financial-news direction prediction across 49,799 articles and 16 model–feature setups (TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, fine-tuned RoBERTa-large/DeBERTa-v3-large, and Llama-3/Qwen2.5 zero/few-shot and LoRA), finding random splits inflate MCC by 1.1×–6.5×, increasing with capacity and feature richness, and that end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning further amplifies the gap (size-matched ratio 1.75×). Under near-chronological evaluation, only M&A shows a positive locked-test signal (TF-IDF MCC 0.138 train-only, 0.068 after train∪val refit; 10,000-permutation p < 10^{-3}), which does not transfer to FNSPID 2009–2020 U.S. data, suggesting localization to 2024–2025 European-tilted M&A semantics. Three role labelers indicate acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, and the authors argue chronological splits purge stale, predictable components, leaving a small, event-localized, lexically shallow residual and call for mandatory leakage audits in financial NLP benchmarks.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It quantifies temporal leakage effects across classic NLP and LLM settings, isolates a regime-specific residual signal, and argues for leakage audits—directly informing robust evaluation protocols for security-relevant LLMs and time-series-oriented foundation models.
